text: The Book of Invasions calls Cesair Ireland's first settler. The account was set down only after Ireland turned to Christianity. The scribes were monks who wanted to present the island as a sacred land. They wove Irish myth together with biblical events. In that version Cesair was the granddaughter of Noah. She fled the Flood by voyaging from the Holy Land. Noah stored beasts in his vessel, while Cesair loaded hers with people, fifty women and three men. She arrived in Ireland four days ahead of the Flood. The waters never covered that ground. Her path wound about. She left Meroe and sailed the length of the Nile. She then came toward the Caspian and Cimmerian seas and over the drowned Alps. Nine days carried her to Spain and nine more brought her to Ireland. She came ashore at Bantry Bay in County Cork. There she portioned the soil among her people. With only three men she made up three bands, each containing a dozen women and a single man. Her father Bith and her brother Ladra died from overmuch sexual strain. Fintan mac Bóchra, the one man left, ran from the pursuing women. The women who traveled with Cesair carried names that harked back to founding mothers, among them German, Espa, Alba, Traige, and Gothiam. Their presence stands for a compact of all the world's peoples. Others echo the goddesses of old Ireland, Banba and Búanann among them. Some writers treat Cesair as a land goddess in her own right. She might be a child of the soil goddess Banba. She may also be Berba, the spirit of the River Barrow, and Heriu, a name close to Ériu. So Cesair could embody each of those divinities. Each of the three men claimed a chief bride. Fintan wed Cesair, Bith wed Bairrind, and Ladra wed Banba, which sets Cesair beside the trio of Banba, Fódla, and Ériu.
